subject: English
framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): English programmes of study, Key Stages 1 to 3, with EYFS Literacy and Communication and Language for Reception
statusNote: The gov.uk English programmes of study (spoken language, reading, writing, KS1 to KS3, plus the KS4 outline) were opened and read. Not opened: the statutory Appendix 1 (spelling) and Appendix 2 (vocabulary, grammar, punctuation) documents, the glossary, and the EYFS statutory framework PDFs (only the gov.uk landing page was read), so the Reception row is provisional. Statutory content is set by key stage (Year 1 and Year 2 individually in KS1; two-year blocks in KS2; KS3 as one block); the year-by-year allocation here is a recommended sequence, and schools may teach content earlier or later within a key stage. Re-check attempt: gov.uk and assets.publishing.service.gov.uk were not reachable from the research environment, so Appendix 1, Appendix 2, the glossary and the EYFS framework could not be opened and no year-by-year spelling or grammar content has been added (it would not be sourced). School-choice notes (not verification gaps): year allocation follows the recommended sequence; Drama, PE, Quran and Arabic links are school subjects outside the English document.

purpose: English is essential to education: pupils must speak, read and write fluently to take part in society.
Reading, especially literature, supports cultural, emotional, intellectual, social and spiritual development.
Pupils should write clearly for different audiences, and use discussion to learn and explain ideas.
Pupils build a wide vocabulary, understand grammar and conventions, and appreciate the literary heritage.

statements: Listen attentively, understand and respond in conversation and stories.
Speak in full sentences, using new vocabulary and talking about experiences.
Ask questions and explain ideas to adults and peers.
Discuss stories and rhymes, and retell them using new vocabulary.
Say sounds for letters and read simple words and sentences using phonics.
Read some common exception words.
Form letters correctly and spell words by saying sounds.
Write simple phrases and sentences that others can read.
Listen and respond to adults and peers; ask relevant questions.
Build vocabulary and articulate and justify answers and opinions.
Give structured descriptions, explanations and narratives.
Take part in collaborative conversation, staying on topic and building on comments.
Use spoken language to speculate, hypothesise and explore ideas.
Speak audibly and fluently in Standard English; take part in drama, presentations and debate.
Consider different viewpoints and select registers for different purposes.
Blend unfamiliar words using known grapheme-phoneme correspondences, including alternative sounds.
Read common exception words and notice unusual spelling-sound links (Year 1).
Read decodable books aloud accurately and reread them for fluency.
In Year 2, read most words without sounding out, and split longer words into syllables.
Listen to and discuss stories, poems and non-fiction above independent reading level.
Retell familiar stories; recite poems by heart; discuss word meanings.
Make inferences, ask and answer questions and predict.
Learn about cause and effect in narrative and non-fiction (Year 2).
Explain clearly their understanding of what is read and heard.
Spell taught phonemes, common exception words and days of the week (Year 1).
Spell with alternative graphemes, homophones, contractions and the singular possessive apostrophe (Year 2).
Add suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful, -less and -ly (Year 2).
Form lower-case letters, capitals and digits correctly; begin joining strokes in Year 2.
Say sentences aloud, compose them orally, then write and reread them.
Sequence sentences into short narratives (Year 1).
Write personal, fictional and real narratives, accounts and poetry (Year 2).
Plan with key vocabulary; proofread for sense and consistent tense.
Use capital letters, full stops, question and exclamation marks.
Join words and clauses using 'and' (Year 1); use subordination and co-ordination (Year 2).
Use statements, questions, exclamations and commands; expanded noun phrases.
Use commas in lists and apostrophes for contractions and singular possession.

keyStages.years: Year 3 to Year 6 (lower: Years 3 to 4; upper: Years 5 to 6)

statements: Use root words, prefixes and suffixes (morphology and etymology) to read and understand new words.
Read further exception words and check unfamiliar pronunciations.
By Year 5, read most words effortlessly and attend to every letter.
Read widely: fiction, poetry, plays, non-fiction, myths and legends, classic and modern texts.
Explain words in context, infer feelings and motives with evidence, and predict.
Summarise ideas across paragraphs; identify how language, structure and presentation shape meaning.
Distinguish fact from opinion; evaluate figurative language (upper KS2).
Prepare and perform poems and plays; learn poetry by heart.
Discuss and challenge views courteously; compare characters, settings and texts.
Spell using prefixes, suffixes, homophones, silent letters and commonly misspelt words.
Use the possessive apostrophe with plural nouns; check spellings in a dictionary.
Write legibly in a joined style, faster and more fluently by Year 6; choose the right implement.
Plan by identifying audience and purpose, using models and research.
Draft with paragraphs, settings, characters, dialogue and organisational devices such as headings.
Evaluate and edit own and others' writing; keep tense consistent; proofread.
Perform compositions with suitable intonation, volume and movement.
Use a wider range of conjunctions, fronted adverbials with commas, and the present perfect (Years 3 to 4).
Punctuate direct speech; begin to notice Standard and non-Standard English.
Use relative clauses, modal verbs, passive verbs and expanded noun phrases (Years 5 to 6).
Use brackets, dashes, colons, semi-colons and hyphens accurately (Years 5 to 6).
Recognise formal and informal structures, including the subjunctive.
Read widely: whole books, short stories, poems and plays from different periods and authors.
Include pre-1914 and contemporary literature, two Shakespeare plays and seminal world literature.
Study at least two authors in depth each year.
Make inferences with evidence; consider purpose, audience and context.
Analyse how language, grammar, structure and organisation create meaning.
Recognise poetic conventions; understand how drama works in performance; compare texts critically.
Write accurately, fluently and at length for many purposes and audiences.
Forms include essays, narratives, scripts, poetry, talks, arguments and letters.
Summarise and organise material; support ideas with factual detail.
Use rhetorical and literary devices from reading.
Plan, draft, edit and proofread; improve coherence.
Extend Appendix 2 knowledge to analyse challenging texts and the effect of grammar.
Use new vocabulary and constructions consciously in writing and speech.
Understand differences between spoken and written language and between registers.
Use Standard English confidently; use linguistic and literary terminology precisely.
Use Standard English in formal and informal contexts, including classroom discussion.
Give short speeches and presentations; take part in formal debates.
Summarise and build on others' points in structured discussion.
Improvise, rehearse and perform scripts and poetry, using role, tone, volume and stillness.
Sets year-by-year spelling patterns, rules and word lists; KS2 has Years 3 to 4 and Years 5 to 6 lists.
Covers prefixes, suffixes, homophones, plurals and common exception words (contents not opened).
Lists the grammatical terms and structures pupils must learn each year.
Pupils learn correct terminology explicitly (detailed contents not opened).

toKS4: KS3 reading, writing, grammar and spoken English prepare pupils for AQA GCSE English Language 8700 and English Literature 8702. For Language, Paper 1 (Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing: AO1, AO2, AO4 reading; AO5, AO6 writing) and Paper 2 (Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives: AO1, AO2, AO3 reading; AO5, AO6 writing) each carry 80 marks and 50%; the Spoken Language endorsement (AO7 to AO9) is reported separately. For Literature, Paper 1 (Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel: 64 marks, 40%) and Paper 2 (Modern texts and poetry: 96 marks, 60%) assess AO1 to AO4. KS3 inference and evidence feed AO1, language and structure analysis feeds AO2, comparison of poems and viewpoints feeds AO3 (Language) and Literature's poetry comparison, context feeds Literature AO3, and the writing and grammar thread feeds AO5, AO6 and Literature AO4. The KS3 requirement for two Shakespeare plays and pre-1914 literature leads to the Paper 1 set texts.
